title: A partner
hook: a chavruta for the long run
tomorrow: same book every year: is the weekly portion a rerun?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Akiva at the well, and a grown man starting with the alef-bet. Choose next year's text. Today, who you read it with.
screen: `CHOOSE NEXT YEAR'S TEXT.` → `WHO YOU READ IT WITH.`

segments.voice: A running partner texts at six in the morning: you up? And somehow you go, on a morning you'd have skipped alone. The Talmud has a strange line about people who skip the partner. It takes a verse from Jeremiah about a sword coming against the boasters, and reads it as a sword against scholars who sit and study by themselves. A sword? For reading alone? That's the odd detail.
screen: `YOU UP?` → `A SWORD AGAINST THE BOASTERS.` → `FOR READING ALONE?`

segments.voice: The answer is a pun. The Hebrew word in the verse, baddim, sounds like bad, alone. So the Talmud says: a sword on those who study alone, and worse, they grow foolish. Not because solitude is wicked. Because alone, nobody pushes back. You read a line, decide what it means, and nobody says: wait, look again. The same page gives the other side. Proverbs says, "Iron sharpeneth iron," and the Talmud reads it as two scholars sharpening each other. That's a chavruta: a study partner. Two people, one text, reading out loud, asking, arguing. Often noisy. And here's the story to tell a friend tonight. The Talmud tells of Choni, who slept so long that when he woke and walked into the study house, nobody believed who he was. Alone and unrecognized, he was miserable, and the Talmud sums it up with a saying: either a study partner, or death. A partner for the long run isn't someone who knows more than you. It's someone who shows up, reads the line beside you, and says what they really think, especially when it isn't what you think.
screen: `BADDIM SOUNDS LIKE 'ALONE'.` · `ALONE, NOBODY PUSHES BACK.` · `IRON SHARPENETH IRON.` · `A PARTNER, OR DEATH.` · then, large: `LEARN IN PAIRS.`

segments.voice: Think of one person who'd be good to learn with: a friend, a parent, a grandparent, anyone who asks good questions. Write them a message inviting them to read one short text with you this week, and name the text. Send it now, or keep it ready for when it feels right.
screen: `ONE PERSON WHO ASKS GOOD QUESTIONS.` · `ONE SHORT TEXT.` · `AN INVITATION.`

segments.voice: A partner: a chavruta, someone who reads the same text beside you for the long run, and pushes back.
Your line: learn in pairs. Iron sharpens iron, and nobody sharpens alone. That's it for today.

screen: `DAY 1745 COUNTS.` → `STUDY FOR LIFE · 3 OF 15.` → `TOMORROW: SAME BOOK EVERY YEAR. IS THE WEEKLY PORTION A RERUN?`

howItsDone: Traditional Jewish study is often done in chavruta, two partners reading a text aloud together, questioning and arguing; study halls are known for the noise of many pairs at once.

chat.meaning: A chavruta isn't a lecture. Two partners sharpen each other, like iron on iron; alone, or silent, nobody pushes back.

chavruta.meaning: a study partner; Aramaic for companionship

baddim.meaning: a word in Jeremiah, read by the Talmud as 'alone ones'

Choni.meaning: a sage in a Talmud story who slept a very long time

Jeremiah.meaning: a prophet; a book of the Hebrew Bible

Talmud.meaning: the vast record of the rabbis' discussions of law and story

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Taanit 7a (Jeremiah 50:36 'a sword upon the baddim' read as scholars who study alone, who grow foolish; Proverbs 27:17 read as two scholars sharpening each other)
Babylonian Talmud, Taanit 23a (Choni wakes, is not recognized in the study house; 'either companionship or death')

notes: Proverbs 27:17 quoted (first words only) from JPS 1917; confirm.
Jeremiah 50:36 paraphrased ('boasters'); the pun baddim/bad is the Talmud's own reading in Taanit 7a (Rabbi Yose bar Chanina). Confirm.

Taanit 23a: the saying 'o chavruta o mituta' is Rava quoting a popular saying about Choni; the script says 'the Talmud sums it up with a saying'. The length of Choni's sleep (seventy years in the source) is left out under the claims rule.
